Partisanship and Polarization in Europe

The notion of polarization has been omnipresent in the literature of the last decade, although (or maybe because of) it is an inherently vague and ambiguous concept.

Whereas earlier research focused on the alignment (or separation) in the broadest sense of ideological positions, be it at the elite or mass level, the seminal contribution by @iyengar2012affect has led to an "affective turn" in the literature.

Highlighting the notion of partisanship as a social identity, affective polarization has originally been defined as the tendency of partisans to like their fellow copartisans and dislike outpartisans, respectively.

Though the on a fundamental level inherently human notion, namely that people like some people more than others, is itself little surprising, the worry was caused more by an observed increase in this affective gap, which has been theorized to hinder political cooperation across party lines, thus ultimately harming the core of democratic life itself.

Since the introduction of affective polarization, a productive research agenda spent vast efforts on studying its causes, consequences, dynamics and measurement itself.

Yet, recent studies call for more cautious interpretations of the underlying group notion attached to the Social Identity Theory (SIT) framework, which served (and still serves) as the theoretical basis for most affective polarization studies (and, therefore, most *polarization* studies in recent years).

Specifically, a recent debate in the American literature called into question if the measured affective gaps between partisans is a consequence of group attachements *per se*, or whether those group attachement serve as a cue signalling a respective policy/ideological position.

The fundamental issue is that both the party-over-policy and policy-over-party accounts yield, for most applied research designs, observationally equivalent outcomes.

What further complicates this issue is that the measurement on partisanship mixes up the terms "affiliation", "attachement", "closeness" and "identity", though each might create different responses.
Few (if any, at this point I haven't seen any) ask directly if respondents *identify* with a party, more commong are question wordings using *attachement* or *feeling close*.
Though beyond the scope of this study, future research could use experimental designs to examine how these various types, all of which aim to capture *emotional/subjective/felt* attachement/identification to a party, yield different response patterns.

In this study, I aim to shed light on the relationship between partisan affiliation (alias *partisanship*) and political polarization in Europe.

Covering multiple facets of ideological and affective polarization, I study how partisanship -- reporting an attachement to a political party -- is associated with different types of polarization.

As a start, I review and summarize the different notions of the term polarization.

I then proceed to summarize the history of the notion of partisanship in Europe.

Empirically, I combine existing data from ongoing large scale survey projects from the European Election Study, the Comparative Study on Electoral Systems and the European Social Survey with a cross-national experimental dataset from 2019.

In a first study, I trace the distribution of partisanship across Euroepean electorates in the first quarter of the 21st century.
Whereas the notion of the "great dealignment" has been the dominant description of the post WW2 period for Western Europe, I try to conceptually disentangle party membership, party affiliation, and stated party preference (via standard vote choice items).
The (preliminary) first impression shows no uniform trend across Europe regarding partisanship, with large variation between different survey project, all of which use slightly different approaches for capturing respondents' feelings of attachement.

In a second study, I investigate the relationship between partisanship and ideological polarization on two dimensions, the left-right and European integration dimension, and the sorting between the two (whether they become more strongly correlated).

In a third study, I take a closer look at how partisanship impacts *perceived* ideological polarization of their respective party systems, on both dimensions, and the perceived sorting of the party system.

In a fourth study, I then turn to affective polarization, specifically *vertical* affective polarization, directed towards parties (as opposed to *partisans*), with *horizontal* attitudinal polarization from the 2024 EES as a complement.

In a fifth study, I compare experimentally measured *horizontal* affective polarization across partisan types.

This study makes multiple contributions: First, it is the most comprehensive study of political polarization in Europe, focusing on its various facets (actual and perceived ideological, vertical and horizontal affective), applying both a dynamic and static lense.



On the term "polarization."
Etymological roots in ancient Europe:
Greek: "Polos" refers to the pivot, axis, or fixed point around which a sphere turns
Latin: Polus (classical) & Polaris (medieval): pertaining to the poles of the earth
French physicist Etienne Louis Malus coined Polariser in early 1800s

physical (light) polarization, magnetism etc.

post WWII: social and political notion, Arthur Koestler, Lipset and Parsons

Typonomy of partisanship

at its core, I use a .

The question is: What is the net contribution of partisanship *itself* on various forms of political polarization?

For this, I focus on the contrast between respondents that do report an attachement (hereafter refered to as explicit partisans) from respondents that *deny* such an attachement, i.e., select the response "No, I don't feel attached to any political party", but report a preference via vote choice items, hereafter refered to as deniers (vote-anchored partisans).
Two further types complete the picture: respondents attached to one party who voted for another (mismatched), and non-partisans.

This contrast allows to estimate the association of partisan attachement with polarization within party (and country), accounting for between-party variation in polarization outcomes.

The key challenge to causal interpretation of this contrast is that partisan attachement is not random -- there are factors correlated with partisan attachement.

If those factors influence both the choice of reporting partisan affiliation and polarization outcomes, this induces counfounding bias, potentially yielding misleading associations between partisan affiliation and polarization.

Hence, in a first step, I review the the notion and history of partisanship in Europe, with a special focus on determinants of partisanship.

Building on this, I examine empirically which variables are associated with reporting a partisanship in the first place, to identify possible (pre-treatment) control variables.

so sequentially its a tree:

| report attachement | report vote | type |
| -- | -- | -- |
| yes | yes, same party | explicit partisan |
| yes | yes, but other party | mismatched (strategic/inconsequential voter?) |
| no | yes | denier (no attachement but preference revealed) |
| no | no | non-partisan |

what makes this of course more complicated: leaner questions, multiple PID.
But (CHECK) many survey start or use binary questions.

So the interesting part is, how do respondents that report attachement differ along multiple polarization dimensions if they have the same partisan anchor compared to those that *deny* such an attachement if directly asked.

The mismatched separate attachment from vote: they share the attachment with explicit partisans of party A and the vote with deniers of party B. The non-partisans have no party of their own; they are a baseline and a diagnostic for selection by the vote.

## Estimation

All outcomes: hierarchical models with respondents in party × country × survey and surveys in countries, plus a time trend where the data are over time. Estimands are contrasts of marginal means computed by g-computation with respondent weights over parties with more than one type. The model is built up step by step (design.md), and the ladder is adjusted as fits come in.

Where one type is rare (e.g. Denmark), the posterior shows this through wider uncertainty. The posterior reflects sampling and the pooling assumptions, not selection or the composition of a group.

### Composition

Share of each of the four types by country and time, with study and wording effects. Descriptive; feeds the decomposition.

### Ideological polarization and sorting

LR primarily, EU also (less data though); over time available.

Extremity $E(|Y - c| \mid t)$ within party, with the centre $c$ still open (scale midpoint, country mean or median: report alternatives). Group quantities (dispersion, bimodality) on each type's predicted distribution with a common party mix.

Sorting: strength of the LR–EU association within a type, whatever its shape (the relation can be an inverted U, and its sign differs between countries), measured within country and pooled as magnitudes.

### Perceived ideological party polarization and sorting

Respondent-level spread of party placements over a fixed party set, LR and EU (where available); over time available. Extension: scale-use-corrected stretch (Bayesian Aldrich–McKelvey). Benchmark: actual positions.

Perceived sorting: how aligned a respondent's LR and EU placements are across parties, against the actual alignment.

### Vertical affective polarization

PTV (EES), like/dislike (CSES), thermometer (eu25); over time available. API primary, other measures robustness. Horizontal attitudinal complement: EES 2024 like/dislike of party supporters.

One row per respondent × rated party, with the relation of the target to the respondent coded as attached and voted / attached only / voted only / neither.

QoI: $AP_t = E(Y \mid Co, t) - E(Y \mid Out, t)$, $\Delta AP = AP_{explicit} - AP_{denier}$; for the mismatched, the attachment-party and the vote-party relation are contrasted within person.

### Horizontal behavioral AP

Dictator/trust games, 2019 only.

QoI as above, plus the split into in-group favoritism $E(Y \mid Co, t) - E(Y \mid Control, t)$ and out-group derogation $E(Y \mid Control, t) - E(Y \mid Out, t)$. Control = a co-national partner with no party shown.

The partner's party is randomized within type (attached respondents were more likely to see a co-partisan), so $AP_t$ is a causal effect of the partner label for each type; $\Delta AP$ is not.

Likelihood: the beta-binomial is ruled out (unimodal, misses the spikes at 0, 5 and 10, cell means off). Current line: the Gaussian on cell means with dispersion by cell, plus an ordinal model as a check of the shape. Acceptance criteria for a new model:

i. It passes the weighted cell-mean and raw-ΔAP checks of notebook 3.5.
ii. It passes the anchor-share checks by cell (3.5) and is calibrated by cell (LOO-PIT, notebook 3.4).
iii. Only then: native LOO among the comparable fits. Cross-family elpd only via the discretization module of 3.4.

## Under what assumptions can this be interpreted as *causal* contrast?

Common to all outcomes: the within-party contrast absorbs everything shared within party × country (platform, status, set of out-parties, elite cues, national norms about admitting an attachment). It does not absorb individual-level confounders of attachment (age and socialization, parental partisanship, interest, ideological intensity). The vote can act as a collider, and self-labelling, wording and vote recall add measurement error. A causal reading needs conditional ignorability of attachment given party × country and pre-treatment covariates, no selection on the outcome through the vote, and a type that means the same across wordings. Triangulating across studies addresses wording, not shared confounding. The three voting types bracket the attachment effect rather than identifying it.

- **Ideology and sorting**: the contrast rules out "attached partisans are in more extreme parties". Reverse causation (ideology -> attachment) is the strongest threat, and selection on proximity makes deniers look less extreme at centrist parties and more extreme at flank parties (diagnostic: type × party position). Read as an association net of party sorting.
- **Perceived polarization and sorting**: the real party system is fixed within a country-survey. Sophistication raises attachment and may make perceived spread more *accurate*; benchmark and scale-use correction narrow this confound, they do not remove it.
- **Vertical AP**: within party plus within person across targets; the mismatched rating of attachment party vs. vote party is the best-identified quantity. Deniers vote for their party partly because they dislike the others, which plausibly pulls ΔAP toward zero. Adjusting for policy distance gives a controlled direct effect, since distance is partly a consequence of attachment.
- **Horizontal behavioral AP**: the partner label is randomized, so $AP_t$ is causal per type; ΔAP is effect heterogeneity by a non-randomized moderator and inherits every confounding problem of type. One election year; few co-partners for deniers.

## Theoretical Implications and Empirical Tests

The explicit–denier contrast ($\Delta$) serves as a diagnostic. The identity
and policy accounts of partisanship predict different *profiles* of $\Delta$
across the polarization outcomes, so the pattern across outcomes
constitutes the test.

Note that these formulated expectations refer to *within* party contrasts; how far that controls for selection and confounding is set out in the section above.

| Outcome | Identity account predicts | Policy account predicts |
|---|---|---|
| Ideological extremity | Small or modest $\Delta$ | Large $\Delta$ (attachment reflects stronger policy commitment) |
| Ideological sorting | to be specified | to be specified |
| Perceived polarization | $\Delta > 0$ beyond actual positions (partisan lens exaggerates distances) | $\Delta$ tracks actual party placements; no excess perception |
| Perceived sorting | to be specified | to be specified |
| Vertical AP (toward parties) | Large $\Delta$, robust to adjusting for policy distance | $\Delta$ shrinks substantially once policy distance is adjusted for |
| Horizontal AP (toward ordinary partisans) | Large $\Delta$, possibly exceeding vertical, since ordinary partisans carry little policy information | Small $\Delta$, since ordinary partisans are weak policy signals |

: Competing predictions of the identity and policy accounts across polarization outcomes {#tbl-predictions}

The tests below form the diagnostic step of the model building.

### Test 1: Estimate $\Delta$ with and without policy adjustment

For each outcome, the within-party contrast is estimated twice: unadjusted,
and conditional on the respondent's own ideological distance to the relevant
parties (left–right, and EU integration where available). The identity
account predicts that the affective $\Delta$s survive adjustment; the policy
account predicts they largely vanish. The central figure is a single
coefficient plot with the four outcomes, each showing both estimates.

### Test 2: Measure perception bias directly

Perceived polarization is constructed relative to a benchmark: sample-mean
placements, expert placements (e.g., Chapel Hill Expert Survey), or
manifesto-based positions. The quantity of interest is whether explicit
partisans' perceived spread *exceeds* the benchmark more than deniers' does.
Greater overestimation among explicit partisans supports
the identity lens.
